PCE price index excluding energy goodsPosted on November 19, 2026

SHARE THIS PAGE:

Link Copied

The takeaway
The St Louis Fed now publishes a PCE price index excluding energy goods, to reduce the volatility in this price index.
The details
Since January 2012, the Federal Reserve has explicitly targeted 2% inflation to meet its price stability mandate. For this purpose, it measures inflation as the 12-month change in the personal consumption expenditures price index (headline PCE).
Headline measures such as this one have volatile components, so policymakers also rely on alternative price indexes that best capture underlying inflationary pressures. For example, Fed officials often refer to inflation “excluding the volatile food and energy categories”, also known as core PCE inflation. However, by excluding food, energy goods, and energy services, core inflation removes a substantial share of consumption expenditures. About 12% on average since 2012.
There is an alternative measure of underlying inflation that removes only energy goods from headline PCE. This preserves the desirable smoothness of core PCE while maintaining a more representative index, by removing a substantially lower share of expenditures than the core version. About 2.6% instead of 12% on average since 2012. A recent blog post describes the case for this index in more detail.
The data
FRED now publishes the series for the PCE price index excluding energy goods. Our first FRED graph, above, shows the constructed price index at a monthly frequency since January 1959. Our second FRED graph, below, compares 12-month inflation when measured by headline PCE and PCE excluding energy goods, focusing on the inflation-targeting era since 2012. As we can see, inflation excluding energy goods is substantially less volatile than headline, but it preserves the broad movements and trends while removing only a small share of expenditures.

How these graphs were created: Search FRED for and select "PCE excluding energy" and you have the first graph. For the second, take the first, click on "Edit Graph," open the "Add Line" tab, search for "PCE price," change units to "percent change from year ago," and adjust the time period.
